description: Thunder, after its flash by the distance over the speed of sound: near, 'a sharp crack or click', far, 'a rumble' (NWS). Its layers are Farnell's (Designing Sound, practical 17): the crack, band-passed noise dying over its decay, heard within the catalog's crack distance; the rumble, low-passed noise swelling and falling swells times a second as the sound of farther stretches of the channel arrives (Glassner 2000: a clap where the channel lies on an arc about the listener, a rumble end-on), held as long as the channel's spread takes the sound to cross and then dying over roll, the echoes off the sea and the cloud; and a deep layer under deep Hz. A flash in its cloud has a channel of stretch metres along the cloud's base (a cloud's channels run kilometres through it: the WMO Cloud Atlas, Glassner 2000). Its energy is mostly 'below 500 Hz', peaking 'at or below 100 Hz' (Johnson 2013). The air absorbs the highs over distance (ISO 9613-1, at 10 °C and 70% humidity, in dB per km at the frequencies given), so a low-pass falls with distance where the absorption reaches 3 dB, within the cutoff's range. A point source: its level falls 6 dB each time the distance doubles from near metres. Distances in metres, frequencies in Hz, times in seconds, levels as gains.
